# Python and C++ for DSA {#sec-lang}

::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- Pick the right container for a task in Python and in C++, and state the true cost of every operation you call on it.
- Use heaps for "repeatedly take the best", including max-heaps in Python, tuple tie-breakers, custom comparators and lazy deletion.
- Sort with keys and comparators, and check that a C++ comparator is a strict weak ordering.
- Answer "largest $\le x$" and "first $\ge x$" queries with `bisect`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` and `multiset`, and simulate a multiset in Python.
- Write programs that read $10^6$ numbers and recurse $10^5$ levels deep without TLE or a crash.
- Avoid integer overflow, floating-point equality, negative remainders, and hash-collision attacks.

## Why this matters

An algorithm only scores when it runs. Between the idea and the accepted verdict sit dozens of small language facts: `list.pop(0)` is linear, `std::set` has no random access, `endl` flushes the output, `-7 % 3` is $-1$ in C++, a Python recursion of depth $10^5$ crashes, and `unordered_map` can be made quadratic by a hacker. None of these is an algorithm, but each one turns a correct solution into **Time Limit Exceeded**, **Runtime Error** or **Wrong Answer**.

Interviews test the same knowledge in a different form. "Implement an LRU cache" is a question about `OrderedDict` or `list` plus iterators. "Top $k$ elements" is a question about heaps. "Why did you use `long long`?" and "What is the complexity of `in` on a list?" are standard follow-ups.

This chapter is the reference for both languages. It first lists the tools and their real costs (Chapter 1's @sec-cx-p6 already covers the basic hidden costs, and @sec-cx-budget the operation budget). Then it turns them into seven patterns, each with fully solved problems in both languages.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
You already know how to solve the problem on paper. This chapter is about the last mile — the handful of small language facts that decide whether a correct idea actually gets accepted. Skim the tables once now and keep them open while you code; come back whenever a submission behaves strangely. You do not have to memorise any of it.
:::

## The Python toolbox {#sec-lang-python}

### Built-in containers

Python hands you four everyday containers for free. Try to pick from this table before you reach for anything fancier.

| Type | What it is | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `list` | dynamic array of references | stacks (`append`/`pop`), indexing, sorting |
| `tuple` | immutable array | dictionary keys, heap entries, multi-key sorting |
| `dict` | hash table, **keeps insertion order** (guaranteed since 3.7) | counting, grouping, memoisation, maps |
| `set`, `frozenset` | hash set | membership, deduplication |
| `str`, `bytes` | immutable sequences | text; build with `"".join(parts)` |
| `int` | arbitrary precision | never overflows, but large values cost $O(\text{digits})$ per operation |

### The `collections` module

When one of the built-ins is *almost* right, the `collections` module usually has the finished version of it.

| Type | Key operations | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `deque` | `append`, `appendleft`, `pop`, `popleft` in $O(1)$; `rotate(k)` | queues, BFS, sliding windows. Indexing the middle is $O(n)$ |
| `Counter` | `Counter(iterable)`, `c[x]` (0 if missing), `most_common(k)`, `c + d`, `c - d` | frequency tables. `c[x]` on a missing key does **not** insert it |
| `defaultdict` | `defaultdict(list)`, `defaultdict(int)` | grouping. Reading `d[x]` on a missing key **inserts** it; use `x in d` or `d.get(x)` to test |
| `OrderedDict` | `move_to_end(k, last=True)`, `popitem(last=False)` | LRU caches: a dict plus a doubly linked list, both operations $O(1)$ |

### `heapq`, `bisect`, `itertools`, `functools`

- **`heapq`** works on a plain list as a binary **min**-heap: `heapify(a)` in $O(n)$, `heappush`, `heappop`, `heappushpop`, `heapreplace` in $O(\log n)$, `a[0]` is the minimum. For a max-heap push `-x`. `nsmallest(k, it)` and `nlargest(k, it)` cost $O(n\log k)$. `heapq.merge(*sorted_iterables)` merges lazily.
- **`bisect`** works on a sorted list: `bisect_left(a, x)` is the first index with `a[i] >= x`, `bisect_right(a, x)` the first index with `a[i] > x`. Both are $O(\log n)$. Since 3.10 they accept `key=`. `insort(a, x)` finds the position in $O(\log n)$ but **inserts in $O(n)$**.
- **`itertools`**: `accumulate` (prefix sums, prefix max with `func=max`), `product`, `permutations`, `combinations`, `combinations_with_replacement`, `groupby` (groups **consecutive** equal keys, so sort first), `pairwise` (3.10+), `chain.from_iterable`, `islice`.
- **`functools`**: `lru_cache(maxsize=None)` or `cache` memoises a function of hashable arguments; `cmp_to_key` turns a two-argument comparator into a sort key; `reduce`.

```{python}
#| label: lang-python-toolbox
c = Counter("mississippi")
assert c.most_common(2) == [("i", 4), ("s", 4)] and c["z"] == 0 and "z" not in c

d = defaultdict(list)
_ = d["missing"]                       # reading inserts an empty list
assert "missing" in d

q = deque([1, 2, 3, 4])
q.rotate(1)
assert list(q) == [4, 1, 2, 3]

h = [5, 1, 4, 2]
heapq.heapify(h)
assert h[0] == 1 and heapq.nsmallest(2, h) == [1, 2] and heapq.nlargest(1, h) == [5]

a = [1, 3, 3, 3, 7]
assert (bisect_left(a, 3), bisect_right(a, 3), bisect_left(a, 4), bisect_right(a, 0)) == (1, 4, 4, 0)

assert list(accumulate([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])) == [3, 4, 8, 9, 14]
assert list(accumulate([3, 1, 4, 1, 5], max)) == [3, 3, 4, 4, 5]
assert [(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby("aaabccaa")] == [("a", 3), ("b", 1), ("c", 2), ("a", 2)]
assert list(pairwise([1, 2, 4])) == [(1, 2), (2, 4)]
assert len(list(combinations(range(5), 2))) == 10 and len(list(permutations(range(4)))) == 24

# Sorting is stable: equal keys keep their input order.
people = [("bob", 25), ("amy", 30), ("cat", 25)]
assert sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]) == [("bob", 25), ("cat", 25), ("amy", 30)]
assert sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])) == [("amy", 30), ("bob", 25), ("cat", 25)]

# Big integers are exact, but converting a huge int to str is capped at 4300 digits (3.11+).
assert 2**100 == 1267650600228229401496703205376
try:
    str(10**5000)
    capped = False
except ValueError:
    capped = True
assert capped
```

### Sorting

`list.sort()` and `sorted()` use Timsort: $O(n\log n)$ worst case, $O(n)$ on already sorted runs, and **stable**. Three ways to say what order you want:

1. **A key function**: `sorted(a, key=len)`. The key is computed once per element.
2. **A tuple key** for several criteria: `key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.name)` sorts by score descending, then name ascending. Negation works only for numbers.
3. **A comparator**: `key=cmp_to_key(cmp)` where `cmp(a, b)` returns a negative number if `a` goes first. Use it only when the order is not a property of each element alone (@sec-lang-p3-largest).

Because the sort is stable, you can also sort by the secondary key first and then by the primary key.

### Strings and big integers

Strings are immutable. `s += t` in a loop *may* be linear in CPython (it resizes in place when nothing else refers to `s`), but this is not guaranteed; collect parts in a list and call `"".join(parts)` once. `s[i:j]` copies $j - i$ characters.

Python integers never overflow, which removes a whole class of bugs. The costs: each `int` object takes 28+ bytes, arithmetic on a $d$-digit number costs $O(d)$ or more, and `str(x)` for $x$ with more than 4300 digits raises `ValueError` unless you call `sys.set_int_max_str_digits(0)`.

## The C++ toolbox {#sec-lang-cpp}

### Containers

C++ splits what Python's single `list` and `dict` do into purpose-built containers. The choice is mostly about one question: do you need the elements to stay **sorted**? If not, reach for the array or the hash table; if yes, reach for the tree.

| Container | Structure | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `vector<T>` | dynamic array | almost everything; `reserve(n)` avoids reallocations |
| `deque<T>` | blocks of arrays | queues, both ends $O(1)$, indexing $O(1)$ |
| `list<T>` | doubly linked list | $O(1)$ `splice`, stable iterators (LRU cache) |
| `set<T>`, `map<K,V>` | red-black tree, sorted | ordered keys, `lower_bound`, predecessor/successor |
| `multiset<T>`, `multimap` | red-black tree with duplicates | sorted bags, sliding-window min/max |
| `unordered_set`, `unordered_map` | hash table with chaining | average $O(1)$ lookups; unsafe on adversarial tests (@sec-lang-p7) |
| `priority_queue<T>` | binary heap over a `vector` | **max**-heap by default; min-heap with `greater<>` |
| `pair`, `tuple`, `array<T,N>` | fixed records | compared lexicographically, usable as `map` keys |

### Binary search in sorted ranges

- `lower_bound(first, last, x)`: first element `>= x`. `upper_bound`: first element `> x`. `equal_range` returns both. They return iterators; subtract `begin()` to get an index.
- On a `set` or `map`, call the **member** function `s.lower_bound(x)`, which is $O(\log n)$. The free function `lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` is $O(n)$ on tree iterators because it cannot jump to the middle.
- "Largest element $\le x$" is `prev(s.upper_bound(x))`, after checking that `s.upper_bound(x) != s.begin()`.

### Comparators and strict weak ordering

`sort`, `set`, `map` and `priority_queue` accept a comparator `comp(a, b)` meaning "`a` goes before `b`". It must be a **strict weak ordering**:

1. **Irreflexive:** `comp(a, a)` is false. So never use `<=` or `>=`.
2. **Transitive:** `comp(a, b)` and `comp(b, c)` imply `comp(a, c)`.
3. **Transitive incomparability:** if `a` and `b` are tied, and `b` and `c` are tied, then `a` and `c` are tied.

Breaking these is undefined behaviour. `std::sort` with `<=` can read outside the array and crash on inputs with many equal elements; a `set` with a bad comparator silently loses or duplicates elements. Python's sort never crashes, but a broken comparator gives an arbitrary order.

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A comparator is just a yes/no answer to "does `a` go before `b`?". The three rules demand that answer be *consistent*: nothing goes before itself, the order has to chain (if `a` beats `b` and `b` beats `c`, then `a` beats `c`), and "these two tie" has to group things cleanly. Break them and C++ is allowed to do anything — usually crash or quietly drop elements. Python won't crash; it just hands you a meaningless order.
:::

`priority_queue<T, vector<T>, Comp>` puts on top the element that is **last** in the order `Comp`. With the default `less<T>`, that is the largest; with `greater<T>`, the smallest. This inversion is why a min-heap comparator uses `>`.

### Iterator invalidation

An iterator (or reference) into a container is a promise about *where* an element lives. Resizing or removing can move elements and silently break that promise — which is why "my loop crashes after an `erase`" is such a common bug. This table says which operations break it:

| Container | Insert | Erase |
|---|---|---|
| `vector`, `string` | all iterators if it reallocates, else those at or after the point | those at or after the point |
| `deque` | all iterators (references stay valid when inserting at either end) | at either end: only the erased; in the middle: all |
| `list`, `set`, `map`, `multiset` | none | only the erased element |
| `unordered_map`, `unordered_set` | all iterators if it rehashes | only the erased element |

The safe erase loop uses the return value: `for (auto it = s.begin(); it != s.end(); ) it = cond(*it) ? s.erase(it) : next(it);`. Never keep a pointer or reference into a `vector` across a `push_back`.

### Modern C++ conveniences

```cpp
map<string, int> cnt;
for (auto& [word, c] : cnt) cout << word << ' ' << c << '\n';     // structured bindings (C++17)
auto [lo, hi] = equal_range(a.begin(), a.end(), x);                  // a pair of iterators
tuple<int, int, int> t{3, 1, 2};
auto [p, q, r] = t;
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const auto& x, const auto& y) {         // sort by (second desc, first asc)
    return tie(y.second, x.first) < tie(x.second, y.first);
});
priority_queue<pair<int, int>, vector<pair<int, int>>, greater<>> pq; // min-heap of pairs
```

### Python and C++ side by side

| Need | Python | C++ |
|---|---|---|
| dynamic array / stack | `list` | `vector` |
| queue / deque | `collections.deque` | `deque` (or `queue`) |
| hash map / set | `dict` / `set` | `unordered_map` / `unordered_set` |
| counting | `Counter` | `unordered_map<T,int>` or `map<T,int>` |
| sorted set with order queries | none in the standard library (sorted list + `bisect`, or a DSU trick) | `set`, `multiset`, `map` |
| min-heap | `heapq` on a list | `priority_queue<T, vector<T>, greater<>>` |
| max-heap | `heapq` with negated keys | `priority_queue<T>` |
| first index `>= x` / `> x` | `bisect_left` / `bisect_right` | `lower_bound` / `upper_bound` |
| LRU order | `OrderedDict` | `list` + `unordered_map` of iterators |
| memoisation | `@lru_cache(maxsize=None)` | array or `map` |
| exact big integers | `int` | `__int128` (to about $1.7\cdot10^{38}$), otherwise hand-written |

## The real cost of each operation {#sec-lang-costs}

These are the tables you keep open while coding. @sec-cx-p6 already flagged the costs that hide inside loops; here is the full picture, so you can look up any operation in one place.

::: {.callout-important title="Python costs (CPython)"}
| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| `list`: `a[i]`, `a[i] = x`, `len`, `append`, `pop()` | $O(1)$ (append amortized) |
| `list`: `pop(0)`, `insert(i, x)`, `del a[i]`, `remove(x)`, `index(x)`, `x in a`, `count` | $O(n)$ |
| `list`: `a[i:j]`, `a + b`, `a * k`, `a[::-1]`, `copy`, `min`, `max`, `sum` | linear in the size of the result or input |
| `list.sort()`, `sorted` | $O(n\log n)$, $O(n)$ if already sorted |
| `dict`/`set`: `get`, `in`, `d[k] = v`, `del`, `add`, `discard` | $O(1)$ average, $O(n)$ worst |
| `set`: union / intersection | $O(\text{len}(s) + \text{len}(t))$ / $O(\min(\text{len}(s), \text{len}(t)))$ |
| `deque`: `append`, `appendleft`, `pop`, `popleft` | $O(1)$ |
| `deque[i]` | $O(1)$ near the ends, $O(n)$ in the middle |
| `heappush`, `heappop`, `heappushpop` / `heapify` | $O(\log n)$ / $O(n)$ |
| `bisect_left`, `bisect_right` / `insort` | $O(\log n)$ / $O(n)$ |
| `Counter(it)` / `most_common(k)` | $O(n)$ / $O(n\log k)$ |
| `"".join(parts)` | $O(\text{total length})$ |
| `str` slicing / `s.find(t)`, `t in s` | $O(\text{length})$ / $O(nm)$ worst case for search |
| `x * y` on $d$-digit ints | about $O(d^{1.58})$ (Karatsuba) |
:::

::: {.callout-important title="C++ costs"}
| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| `vector`: `[]`, `back`, `push_back`, `pop_back`, `size` | $O(1)$ (push amortized) |
| `vector`: `insert`/`erase` in the middle or front, `find` | $O(n)$ |
| `deque`: push/pop at both ends, `[]` | $O(1)$ |
| `list`: `insert`, `erase`, `splice` at an iterator | $O(1)$ |
| `set`/`map`: `insert`, `erase`, `find`, `count`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` | $O(\log n)$ |
| `multiset::count(x)` | $O(\log n + k)$ where $k$ = copies of $x$ |
| `multiset::erase(x)` (by value) | erases **all** copies |
| `next`, `prev`, `distance` on tree iterators | $O(1)$ amortized per step; `distance` is $O(n)$ |
| `unordered_map`: `find`, `[]`, `insert`, `erase` | $O(1)$ average, $O(n)$ worst (@sec-lang-p7) |
| `priority_queue`: `push`, `pop` / `top` / build from range | $O(\log n)$ / $O(1)$ / $O(n)$ |
| `sort` / `stable_sort` / `nth_element` | $O(n\log n)$ / $O(n\log n)$ / $O(n)$ average |
| `string`: `+= c`, `push_back` / `s = s + t` / `substr(i, k)` | $O(1)$ amortized / $O(\text{len}(s) + \text{len}(t))$ / $O(k)$ |
| passing a container **by value** | $O(n)$ copy; pass `const&` |
| `endl` | writes `'\n'` **and flushes** |
:::

::: {#fig-lang-costs}

```{python}
#| echo: false
```
